Abel.note: A Hebrew name, indeclinable in Latin. The second son of Adam, whose offering of sheep was accepted where Cain's was not (Gen 4).

Abraham.note: A Hebrew name. Latin gives it a genitive and dative Ábrahæ and otherwise leaves it indeclinable.

Agatha.note: A Greek name, “good”. The Sicilian martyr named in the Canon.

Agnes.note: A Greek name, “pure”. The Roman martyr named in the Canon.

Anastasia.note: A Greek name, “resurrection”. The martyr named in the Canon.

Baptista.note: A masculine 1st-declension noun, like agrícola — farmer.

Barnabas.note: The name the Apostles gave him. Acts 4:36 renders it “son of consolation”.

Bartholomaeus.note: An Aramaic name — bar-Talmai, “son of Talmai”.

Caecilia.note: A Roman martyr, and the patroness of church music.

Christus.note: Greek Christós — “the anointed one” — rendering Hebrew Mashiach (Messiah).

Cornelius.note: The name of an old Roman gens.

Cosmas.note: A Greek name, “order”. A physician, martyred in Cilicia with Damian.

Cyprianus.note: “Of Cyprus”, from the Latin name of the island.

Damianus.note: A physician, martyred in Cilicia with Cosmas.

Elias.note: The prophet Elijah, in the spelling the Douay-Rheims and this edition's verses use. Latin took the form from the Greek of the Septuagint.

Eva.note: The name of the first mother, Hebrew for the living one.

Ierosolyma.note: The city's declinable name, neuter plural. The indeclinable form stands at Ierusalem.

Iesus.note: Through Greek from the Hebrew name Yeshua — “God saves”. Irregular declension (nominative Iesus, accusative Iesum, all other cases Iesu).

Ignatius.note: The third Bishop of Antioch, martyred at Rome.

Ioannes.note: From Hebrew Yochanan — “the Lord is gracious”.

Ioseph.note: A Hebrew name. This edition leaves it indeclinable, though a witness it collates prints the ablative Iosepho.

Isaias.note: The prophet Isaiah, in the spelling the Douay-Rheims and the Vulgate use. Latin took the form from the Greek of the Septuagint.

Israel.note: The name given to Jacob at Genesis 32:28 — because he was strong against God.

Laurentius.note: From Laurentum, a town in Latium.

Linus.note: The first martyr named in the Canon after the Apostles.

Lucia.note: From lux, “light” — the name of one born at daybreak.

Marcellinus.note: From Marcellus, itself a diminutive of Marcus.

Matthaeus.note: A shortened Hebrew name — “gift of the Lord”.

Matthias.note: The apostle chosen to take the place of Judas (Acts 1:23–26).

Melchisedech.note: Christian tradition sees in Melchisedech, the “priest of God Most High” (Gen. 14:18), a prefiguration of Christ's priesthood (CCC 1544).

Michael.note: From Hebrew Mika'el — “Who is like God?”.

Petrus.note: Aramaic Cephas means “rock”. In John 1:42 the Evangelist interprets it with Greek Pétros.

Pilatus.note: A Roman surname, borne by the governor of Judaea in the time of Jesus.

Pontius.note: The name of a gens, Samnite before it was Roman.

Simon.note: A Greek name that stood in for the Hebrew Simeon.

Stephanus.note: The first martyr of the Church (Acts 6:8–7:60).

Thaddaeus.note: An Aramaic name. The lexicons record the form and leave the meaning open.

Thomas.note: John gives the Greek byname as well — Dídymus, “twin”.

Xystus.note: Pope Sixtus II, martyred at Rome in 258. The Canon names him and not his earlier namesake.

ab.note: Usually a before a consonant, ab before a vowel or h.

ac.note: The form of atque used before a consonant.

adscribo.note: Literally, to write in beside or enter on a list.

advocata.note: The feminine of advocátus — one called to another's side (ad and voco) to stand by the accused.

agnus.note: Ecce Agnus Dei — the Baptist's words about Christ (John 1:29).

ago.note: In the phrase grátias ágere it means “to give thanks”.

alius.note: Declines like a pronoun: genitive alíus, dative álii — not like the -us, -a, -um adjectives.

alleluia.note: Hebrew hallelu-Yah — “praise the Lord”. The word passed through Greek and is indeclinable in Latin.

altare.note: The plural altária is common in classical Latin. The singular altáre also occurs regularly in the Vulgate and the liturgy.

altus.note: Altíssimus is the superlative of altus: “the Most High.”

amen.note: A Hebrew word, indeclinable in Latin.

amputo.note: From am- (for ambi-, around) and putare, to cut or prune.

angelus.note: Greek ángelos means “messenger”. The word entered Latin through Greek.

antistes.note: Literally, one who stands before. In Christian Latin it is a title for a bishop.

audeo.note: A semi-deponent: the present system is ordinary and active, the perfect passive in form and active in meaning (ausus sum, I dared).

aufero.note: The case name ablative comes from ablátum, “taken away”.

autem.note: It never stands first in its sentence — normally after the first word, sometimes after a word-group taken as one (In diébus autem illis).

baptisma.note: A neuter Greek loanword. Genitive baptísmatis.

benedico.note: A compound of bene (well) and dico (I say).

beneficium.note: From bene (well) and facio (I do): a good done for someone.

catholicus.note: From Greek katholikós — “universal,” in the sense of “according to the totality” or “in keeping with the whole.”

cherubim.note: A Hebrew plural. The singular is cherub. It is indeclinable in Latin. The Vulgate treats it as masculine, duos cherubim aureos in Exodus 25:18. The common preface puts Séraphim in the neuter, beáta Séraphim.

concupisco.note: An -sco formation on cupio — the shape Latin uses for beginnings — lexicalized as strong desire itself: to long for, to covet. The same root as concupiscence.

conspectus.note: “In conspéctu” means before the face of, in the presence of.

consubstantialis.note: In the Creed, it means that the Son is of the same substance as the Father.

converto.note: The passive often has a reflexive sense: “to turn oneself toward someone.”

credo.note: With the dative of a person: credo tibi, I believe you. With in and the accusative: I believe in someone.

senses: when (as a conjunction, with the indicative)

de.note: De can mark separation or motion from above. Ex often marks motion from within.

deus.note: In the Vulgate and liturgical Latin, the vocative has the same form as the nominative: Deus.

dextera.note: Understand “(manus) déxtera” — the right hand. “At the right hand” is Scripture's place of honor.

dies.note: One of the few 5th-declension nouns. Usually masculine, feminine especially of an appointed day.

dignor.note: A deponent verb from dignus — worthy. Dignéris means “be pleased to”.

domus.note: It has forms from both the fourth and second declensions.

dono.note: It most often takes the thing in the accusative and the person in the dative.

ecce.note: A pointing interjection. Standing alone it takes the nominative (ecce homo). It can also point at a whole sentence — then the noun after it may be the object of its own verb.

eleison.note: Greek ἐλέησον, the imperative of ἐλεέω, “to have mercy”.

enim.note: Never stands first in its clause: Latin slips it into second, less often third place.

eo.note: An irregular verb. Plural imperative: ite.

eucharistia.note: A Greek noun, “the giving of thanks”.

ex.note: Before a vowel always “ex”. Before a consonant both “e” and “ex” occur (ex María Vírgine).

exaudio.note: In prayer it can mean to hear favorably, not merely to hear.

facio.note: In the present system its passive is supplied by fio (to become). The perfect passive is factus sum.

fidelis.note: In the plural it stands as a noun: fidéles, the faithful.

finis.note: In the plural fines means boundaries, and hence the territory they enclose.

fio.note: Irregular. Serves as the passive of “fácere”, to do or make, in the present system — the perfect passive is factus sum.

futurus.note: The future participle of sum. Neuter plural futura means “things to come”.

gaudeo.note: A semi-deponent: active forms in the present system and passive forms in the perfect system, e.g. gavísus sum — “I rejoiced”.

genetrix.note: A noun from gigno, to beget. The spelling genitrix also occurs.

gigno.note: The present stem is reduplicated (gi-gn-o) beside the root gen- seen in génui and génitum.

hic.note: The demonstrative of what is near the speaker. Not to be confused with the adverb hic — here.

hic_adverbium.note: The adverb of place. Not the demonstrative hic, hæc, hoc — this.

hosanna.note: A Hebrew cry from Ps 117:25, taken up by the crowd greeting Christ in Mt 21:9. Latin retains it untranslated. The word is indeclinable.

idem.note: It is the pronoun is with the ending -dem. Before d the m turns to n (eúndem).

igitur.note: A postpositive particle: it does not usually stand first in its clause.

impero.note: Takes the dative for the person commanded.

senses: before (in conspéctu — in the sight of)

indulgentia.note: In Church terminology, it means an indulgence: remission before God of temporal punishment for sins whose guilt has already been forgiven.

indulgeo.note: It governs the dative of the person: indulgére alicui — to be gracious to someone.

inferi.note: Used substantivally in the plural. Ab ínferis means “from among the dead”.

institutio.note: From instítuere, to set up or establish.

intellectus.note: From intellégere, to understand, grasp, or discern.

intro.note: A verb. Not to be confused with the identically spelt adverb intro — “inwards.”

introeo.note: A compound of intro and eo. It inflects irregularly like eo.

invoco.note: Scripture frequently uses invocáre nomen Dómini — “to call upon the name of the Lord.”

ipse.note: An intensive pronoun emphasizing the person or thing spoken of.

iste.note: In Classical Latin, it usually points to a person or thing associated with the addressee.

iucundus.note: Related to iuváre, to help or please.

iustificatio.note: In the Psalter, plural iustificationes means God's statutes or ordinances.

kyrie.note: Greek κύριε, the vocative of κύριος, “Lord”.

lacryma.note: Lacryma and lacrima are spelling variants of the same word.

laetor.note: A deponent verb: passive in form but active in meaning.

lex.note: In Psalm 118, Latin lex corresponds to Hebrew torah, a word that means both law and instruction.

liber.note: Not the noun liber, libri (“book”) or líberi, liberórum (“children”).

liber_volumen.note: Not the adjective liber, líbera, líberum (“free”), which stands under its own head.

martyr.note: Greek mártys means “witness”. A martyr bears supreme witness to Christ, even unto death.

memini.note: A defective verb: it has only perfect-system forms, but a present sense. Its only imperatives are future: meménto, plural mementóte.

mereor.note: A deponent verb: passive in form but active in meaning.

misereor.note: Normally with the genitive (miserére mei, misereátur vestri). Liturgical formulas also use the dative (miserére nobis).

miseror.note: A deponent verb: passive in form but active in meaning.

mortuus.note: The perfect participle of mórior (to die), used both as an adjective and as a noun: mórtui, the dead.

senses: lest, that … not (opening a negative purpose clause)

nec.note: The phrase nec non means “and also”.

neque.note: The same word as nec in its full shape.

offero.note: A compound of ob- and fero. It is conjugated irregularly like fero.

orbis.note: Orbis terrárum — “the circle of the lands,” meaning “the world.”

oro.note: The call “Orémus” — let us pray — is the same verb.

os.note: Not os, ossis (“bone”). The two nouns share a nominative form but have different stems.

patior.note: From the participle passus comes pássio — suffering, the Passion.

patriarcha.note: A masculine noun of the first declension.

senses: to bring all the way to

perhibeo.note: Often used in the phrase testimónium perhibére, “to bear witness”.

pervagor.note: A deponent verb: passive in form but active in meaning.

placeo.note: It governs the dative of the person: to be pleasing to someone.

senses: full of (with the ablative or genitive)

praeclarus.note: The prefix præ- is intensive here.

prex.note: Most often used in the plural: preces. The singular nominative is not used.

pridie.note: Prídie Kaléndas means the day before the first of the month.

senses: by reason of (the ground of a petition)
to proceed, to come forth from

propheta.note: A masculine noun of the first declension.

proprius.note: In the liturgy, the proprium comprises the texts proper to a particular day or observance.

prosum.note: A compound of sum. Before a form beginning with a vowel, d appears: prodest, prodésse. It takes the dative.

quaeso.note: A defective verb. Chiefly the forms quæso and quǽsumus survive, used in requests.

quis.note: After si, nisi, ne and num, quis usually has the indefinite sense ‘someone’ or ‘something’.

quoque.note: It usually follows the word it belongs to.

quotidianus.note: In the Lord's Prayer, quotidiánus corresponds to Greek epioúsios. The Vulgate has supersubstantiálem at Mt 6:11 and quotidiánum at Lk 11:3.

quotquot.note: An indeclinable relative with plural meaning.

refrigerium.note: Literally, a cooling. In prayer for the dead: refreshment and rest.

refugium.note: The noun of refúgio, to flee for help. It can also denote a place of refuge.

reliquiae.note: A noun used in the plural.

senses: release from a debt or penalty

sabaoth.note: Sabaoth is an indeclinable transcription of a plural Hebrew noun meaning ‘hosts’. In Deus Sabaoth it means ‘God of Hosts’.

saeculum.note: In the phrase in sǽcula sæculórum, repetition intensifies the sense: “unto the ages of ages”.

salutare.note: The adjective salutáris (saving) used as a noun.

salveo.note: The imperatives salve and salvéte are forms of greeting, singular and plural respectively.

satanas.note: A masculine noun of the first declension.

scrutor.note: The verb denotes close, careful examination. The name Scrutabor comes from its form scrutábor.

seraphim.note: A Hebrew plural. The singular is seraph. It is indeclinable in Latin.

socius.note: Used as a noun, sócius means ‘companion’.

species.note: In a Eucharistic context this denotes the outward sacramental appearance. The Latin morphology determines number because English species has one form for singular and plural.

spero.note: In the sense “to trust”, it can take in with the ablative: speráre in Deo — to put one's hope in God.

senses: in the time of, under (a ruler)
to come to the aid of

sui.note: The reflexive pronoun has no nominative. The same forms refer to singular and plural subjects.

sumo.note: With reference to Communion, sumere means “to receive”.

suspicor.note: A deponent verb: passive in form and active in meaning.

suus.note: The reflexive possessive, normally referring to the subject of its clause.

tantum.note: The neuter accusative of tantus, used adverbially.

tenebrae.note: The noun is used only in the plural.

totus.note: Its genitive is totíus and its dative toti — a pronominal declension, not the ordinary adjectival one.

tristis.note: A two-termination adjective: one form for masculine and feminine (tristis), another for neuter (triste).

una.note: An adverb formed from the ablative of unus. Una cum means ‘together with’.

unus.note: It takes pronominal endings in the genitive (uníus) and the dative (uni).

ut.note: With the subjunctive it means so that. With the indicative, as.

uti.note: An older form of ut. Not to be confused with the infinitive of utor.

veneror.note: A deponent: passive in form, active in meaning.

venter.note: In the received English of the Ave María the word is “womb”: “fruit of thy womb”.

vester.note: The possessive of the second person plural. Its form vestri also serves as the genitive of the pronoun vos.

via.note: In Psalm 118, via is an image for a way of life.

vir.note: Vir is a male. Homo is a human being of either sex.

viscus.note: Usually plural: víscera. It denotes the internal organs and, figuratively, what is innermost.

vivus.note: Used as a noun: vivi, the living.

volo.note: An irregular verb with neither passive forms nor a supine.

vos.note: Its genitive has two shapes: vestri (objective, as in misereátur vestri) and vestrum (partitive).
